title: Savings that hurt: Production rationalization and its effect on prices
abstract: Abstract Postmerger scenarios often lead to a reallocation of resources and production across the merged entity. Production rationalization, the process of reallocating production across facilities so as to reduce total costs, results in firms equating marginal costs across markets. This results in marginal costs, and hence prices, being higher in some markets and lower in others than otherwise would be without production rationalization. This paper proposes a model of competition that elicits these effects and the resulting consequences on consumer and producer surplus. The paper also presents empirical evidence to show that production rationalization, in the form of fleet reoptimization, affected prices following the US Airways/American Airlines merger. Prices of the merged firm increased 10% on routes typically served by US Airways relative to routes typically served by American Airlines, and by 12% relative to US Airways’ rivals’ prices. Price‐cost regressions confirm such price hikes were likely due to fleet reoptimization.

summary.oneLiner: Merged firms reallocating production to cut costs can raise prices in some markets; after the US Airways/American merger, fares rose about 10-12% on certain routes.
summary.overview: When two companies merge, they often shift production across their facilities to save money, a process called production rationalization. The authors argue this equalizes marginal costs (the cost of producing one more unit) across markets, which can push prices up in some markets even as costs fall overall. They build a model of competition to show these effects and their impact on consumer and producer surplus (the value consumers and firms gain from trade). Using the US Airways and American Airlines merger, they present empirical evidence that fleet reoptimization, a form of production rationalization, raised prices on certain routes.
summary.question: Does reallocating production across facilities after a merger, specifically production rationalization, lead to higher prices in some markets, and what are the effects on consumer and producer surplus?
summary.method: The paper proposes a model of competition to show how production rationalization affects prices and welfare. It also presents empirical evidence on fleet reoptimization following the merger, using price comparisons and price-cost regressions.

findings: Production rationalization results in firms equating marginal costs across markets, so marginal costs and hence prices are higher in some markets and lower in others than otherwise would be.
Following the US Airways/American Airlines merger, prices of the merged firm increased 10% on routes typically served by US Airways relative to routes typically served by American Airlines.
Prices of the merged firm increased 12% relative to US Airways' rivals' prices on those routes.
Price-cost regressions confirm such price hikes were likely due to fleet reoptimization.
summary.whyItMatters: The paper implies that cost savings from post-merger reallocation of production can come at a cost to consumers in some markets, so the net effect of a merger on prices depends on where production is shifted. Competition and merger policy should account for this mechanism, since cost reductions alone do not guarantee lower prices.
